summary: In this episode of the Lord of Spirits, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen DeYoung explore the topic of ritual purity and uncleanness in the Old Testament and its continued relevance in Orthodox Christian practice. They begin by distinguishing between moral uncleanness, which results from sin and makes one unfit to approach God, and ceremonial or ritual uncleanness, which arises from unavoidable bodily functions, touching unclean things, or contact with death, and is not inherently sinful. They emphasize that the clean/unclean distinction is not about good versus evil but about holy versus common, and that ritual uncleanness is a normal part of life that requires purification before approaching God. The hosts then discuss how these concepts persist in the New Testament and the Orthodox Church, including the practice of churching mothers and infants, the preparation of clergy, and the ongoing need for purification before receiving the Eucharist. They also address common misunderstandings, such as conflating ritual impurity with sin, and critique both the tendency to dismiss these practices as obsolete and the opposite error of over-spiritualizing every aspect of life. The episode concludes with a reflection on the purpose of purification: to enable intimacy with God, and the importance of balancing the holy and the common in Christian life.

entities.title: Cain
entities.summary: The archetypal morally unclean person in Second Temple Judaism, whose murder of Abel and subsequent curse made him permanently unclean and alienated from creation.

entities.title: Book of Leviticus
entities.summary: The primary source for laws of clean and unclean, including the distinction between holy and common, and the procedures for purification.

entities.title: Josephus
entities.summary: First-century Jewish historian who described Cain as 'the most evil' and discussed the permanent impurity of those who shed blood in the temple.

entities.title: Philo of Alexandria
entities.summary: Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who wrote about the permanent ritual impurity of murderers and their inability to perform sacred functions.

entities.title: King David
entities.summary: Example of repentance and acceptance of permanent ritual impurity, as he was not allowed to build the temple due to bloodshed, yet his sin was forgiven.

entities.title: Theotokos (Virgin Mary)
entities.summary: The Mother of God, whose giving birth without corruption is celebrated in the feast of the Purification, and whose example is followed in the churching of mothers.

concepts.title: Moral Uncleanness
concepts.summary: Uncleanness resulting from sin, such as murder, sexual immorality, or idolatry, which makes one unfit to approach God and requires repentance and purification.

concepts.title: Ceremonial (Ritual) Uncleanness
concepts.summary: Uncleanness from unavoidable bodily functions, touching unclean things, or contact with death, which is not sinful but requires ritual washing before approaching God.

concepts.title: Holy vs. Common
concepts.summary: The distinction between things set apart for God (holy) and ordinary things (common), which is the proper framework for understanding clean and unclean, rather than good and evil.

concepts.title: Sin Offering
concepts.summary: A sacrifice offered upon reentry into the community after a period of uncleanness, which deals with sins committed during the separation, not the uncleanness itself.

concepts.title: Agos (Accursed)
concepts.summary: A Greek term for a state of permanent ritual impurity resulting from extreme moral crimes, such as murder, which bars one from sacred functions for life.

concepts.title: Churching of Mother and Child
concepts.summary: Orthodox practice of prayers for purification and reentry into the church after childbirth, rooted in Leviticus 12 and the presentation of Christ in the temple.

claims.text: Nothing in the Old Testament is simply dropped with the coming of Christ; rather, it is transformed or persists in the New Covenant.
Clean and unclean in the Old Testament are not equivalent to good and evil; they refer to holy versus common, and ritual uncleanness is not sinful.
Ceremonial uncleanness is largely unavoidable in daily life, arising from bodily functions, touching unclean things, and contact with death, and is not a moral failing.
The sin offering required after a period of uncleanness is for sins committed during the separation, not for the uncleanness itself, which is not sinful.
Certain extreme sins, like murder, can result in permanent ritual impurity in this life, barring one from sacred functions, even after repentance and forgiveness.
Baptism uniquely washes away moral uncleanness, unlike ritual washings which only address ceremonial impurity, and is therefore done only once.
In the New Covenant, the distinction between holy and common remains; not everything is holy, and common things are not inherently bad.
